sections.h2: How is New Hampshire divided for property sellers?
sections.html:
New Hampshire has 10 counties, 13 cities, 221 towns and 25 unincorporated places, according to the state's government directory. For a seller the town or city is the unit that matters most, because property is assessed and taxed locally, while the county runs the registry of deeds where your deed is recorded.

The state's regions are commonly named as the Great North Woods, the White Mountains, the Lakes Region, the Seacoast, the Merrimack Valley, the Monadnock region and Dartmouth-Lake Sunapee. Those regions are not government units. When you read a guide on this site, look for the town and the county together.

sections.h2: Who assesses and collects property tax in New Hampshire?
sections.html:
Cities and towns do. The Department of Revenue Administration says local property taxes are assessed, levied and collected by municipalities from owners of New Hampshire property, and its Property Bureau monitors assessing practices statewide. The governing law is RSA 76 and the department's Rev 600 rules.

Three dates organize the year for an owner:

  • April 1: the property tax year runs April 1 to March 31, and taxes are assessed on the inventory taken in April (RSA 76:2).
  • July 1 and December 1: in towns and cities that bill semiannually, a partial payment is due July 1 and the remainder December 1 (RSA 76:15-a).
  • April 15: the deadline to file a permanent application for exemptions and tax credits (RSA 72:33).

If a town denies an exemption, the owner can appeal to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals or superior court no later than September 1 following the notice of tax, with a nonrefundable $65 filing fee payable to the Treasurer, State of New Hampshire.

Because every municipality sets its own rate and adopts its own exemption amounts, two houses of equal value in neighboring towns can carry different bills. Check the municipal tax collector for the current figure before you list or sign a contract.

sections.h2: What does a transfer cost when a house sells?
sections.html:
The state transfer tax is $.75 per $100 of the price or consideration, with a $20 minimum when the price is $4,000 or less (RSA 78-B:1). On a $400,000 sale that rate works out to $3,000, and the statute computes the tax to the nearest whole dollar.

On top of that, a $25 surcharge funds the Land and Community Heritage Investment Program, known as LCHIP. LCHIP says the surcharge is assessed on four types of documents recorded at county registries of deeds, under RSA 478:17-g, and it has produced an average of $4,000,000 to $4,500,000 a year. The registry also charges its own recording fees, which differ by county, so ask the registry for its current schedule.

These figures belong in your net sheet whether you sell on the open market or to a cash buyer. Our team reviews them with sellers before closing so the number on the offer matches the number at the table.

sections.h2: Where are New Hampshire deeds recorded?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded at the county registry of deeds. The Registry of Deeds is a county government office that maintains public records, especially records relating to real estate ownership, and the state directory lists one for each of the 10 counties.

Hillsborough County is the unusual case worth knowing about, since it has two seats, Manchester and Nashua. Rockingham County's seat is Brentwood. Several counties publish their registries on nhdeeds.org, while Carroll and Merrimack use their own county sites. A title company normally handles the recording, but a seller who is checking an old lien or a probate transfer can search the registry directly.

sections.h2: What protections and exemptions should a seller know about?
sections.html:
Two statewide rules come up often: the homestead right and local property tax exemptions. The homestead right under RSA 480:1 protects up to $400,000 of a person's homestead from creditors, with a 6-month window to reinvest sale proceeds in a new primary residence. Property tax exemptions for the elderly, blind, disabled and veterans are adopted by each municipality under RSA 72, so the amounts differ from town to town.

Our separate homestead exemption page explains both in detail. For a seller the practical points are to file an amended application by December 1 after you change residence if you hold an exemption, and to tell the assessor about the sale.

sections.h2: What rules govern selling a rented house in New Hampshire?
sections.html:
The landlord and tenant rules are statewide, found in RSA 540 and RSA 540-A, and they do not change by county. Residential eviction notices are 30 days in general and 7 days for nonpayment, substantial damage or behavior that harms health or safety (RSA 540:3). A landlord must get a judge's permission before a typical tenant has to leave, and only a sheriff can carry out the writ of possession.

The Judicial Branch also runs a mediation program that can be reached at 603-271-6418.

Our eviction notice and eviction process pages break the steps down. If you do not want to wait through them, we buy New Hampshire houses as-is, including houses with tenants.

sections.h2: What should a seller check first, county by county?
sections.html:
The checklist is the same everywhere, but the office you call changes with the county and the town. Here is where each piece sits.

  • Tax bill status: the municipal tax collector in the town or city where the house stands, not the county.
  • Liens and prior deeds: the registry of deeds for the county. Hillsborough County has two county seats, Manchester and Nashua, and Rockingham County's seat is Brentwood.
  • Exemptions: the town or city assessors, who take the permanent application by April 15. Manchester's assessors publish their exemption and credit amounts online.
  • Tenants: the circuit court clerk for the area where the house is, plus the statewide mediation line at 603-271-6418.
  • Inherited houses: the probate steps, which we cover in our separate New Hampshire probate guide.

Size does not change the statutes. Hillsborough County had 422,937 residents in the 2020 Census and Coös had 31,268, yet the same RSA 76 assessment calendar, the same RSA 78-B transfer tax and the same RSA 540 eviction notices apply in both. What changes is the local office, its hours and its adopted exemption amounts. Call the town or city office first, confirm what it needs in writing, and keep copies of every form you file. We can walk through any of these steps with you on a call, and we buy New Hampshire houses as-is when you would rather skip them.

faqs.q: How many counties and towns does New Hampshire have?
faqs.a: New Hampshire has 10 counties, 13 cities, 221 towns and 25 unincorporated places, according to the state's government directory.

faqs.q: Who sets property tax in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: Each city or town assesses, levies and collects its own property tax under RSA 76. The Department of Revenue Administration monitors assessing practices statewide.

faqs.q: What is the New Hampshire real estate transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: The rate is $.75 per $100 of price or consideration, with a minimum tax of $20 when the price is $4,000 or less (RSA 78-B:1).

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: At the registry of deeds in the county where the property sits. The state directory lists one registry for each of the 10 counties.

faqs.q: Is there a state eviction timeline that applies in every county?
faqs.a: The notice rules are statewide: 30 days generally and 7 days for nonpayment, substantial damage or health and safety behavior. Court calendars are handled by the clerk of the circuit court that hears your case.
